title: The horse is handsome, not you
hook: don't boast about your fine horse, as if its beauty were yours (Enchiridion 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: dogma, the judgment underneath the upset. Your line was it's my view. When something stung, did you split it in two? Day three hundred thirty-eight.

A man pulls into a parking lot in a very shiny car and takes a little longer than necessary to get out of it. A parent mentions, for the third time at dinner, which college the kid got into. A fan says we won last night, about a team he has never played for. Each one is standing next to something fine and letting a little of its shine land on them. Epictetus noticed it in the ancient equivalent: the man with the beautiful horse. Today: the horse is handsome, not you.
screen: `THE SHINY CAR.` → `WE WON LAST NIGHT.` → `THE MAN WITH THE BEAUTIFUL HORSE.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. Section six of the handbook says: don't be lifted up by an excellence that isn't yours. Second, the joke inside it. If the horse itself were proud, Epictetus says, and announced, I am beautiful, that would be bearable. The horse is, after all, beautiful. But when you say, I have a beautiful horse, and puff up, you're proud of the horse's good, not yours. The mane, the speed, the gleam: those belong to the animal. You're just the one holding the rope. Third, his question. So what is yours? His answer is a short phrase: the use of impressions. Every moment, things appear to you, a horse, an insult, a compliment, a fear. What you do with those appearances, how you judge them and respond, that's yours. When you handle them well, in line with nature, he says, then go ahead and be glad, because then you're glad about a good that's really your own. Fourth, why it matters on a Tuesday. Borrowed pride is fragile. The car gets scratched. The team loses. The kid has a hard year and suddenly your sense of yourself wobbles along with theirs. Epictetus isn't saying don't enjoy the horse, or don't love the kid, or don't cheer. He's saying keep the accounts straight. The horse is handsome. Your part is what you did today with what showed up. That can't be scratched in a parking lot.
screen: `AN EXCELLENCE NOT YOUR OWN.` · `IF THE HORSE SAID I AM BEAUTIFUL.` · `YOURS: THE USE OF IMPRESSIONS.` · `BORROWED PRIDE IS FRAGILE.` · then, large: `THE HORSE IS HANDSOME.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you feel a little proud of that isn't strictly yours. A possession, a title, where you went to school, a famous relative, a city, a team. Picture it clearly. Then give the credit back with Epictetus' sentence: the horse is handsome. Say the real name in place of horse. Notice whether anything in you shrinks or relaxes. Then ask: what did I actually do this week that was mine? Let one small answer come. The bell holds the time.
The horse is handsome. Epictetus' reminder that the shine of what we own or stand near belongs to it, not to us; ours is how we meet things. Today's word.
Your line: the horse is handsome. Catch one borrowed pride today, in yourself, gently. Say the line, and let the horse keep its own shine. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism notice when they take credit for something they merely own or stand near, and remind themselves that their own part is how they respond.

fork.setup: someone admires your beautiful horse. what does Epictetus have you notice?
options: that you chose well, so the credit is yours.
that the beauty belongs to the horse.
that you should sell it before it ages.
fork.reveal: the excellence is the horse's. be glad about your own good: how you handle what appears to you.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be a show-off.
what it means: don't take pride in an excellence that isn't yours; take it in how you meet what appears.
what a scholar hears: 'the use of impressions' (chresis phantasion) is the phrase section six gives for what is really ours.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): removed 'we all do some version of this' (an 'all' claim about the listener) and the unsourced claim that the phrase 'runs all through his teaching'.
Enchiridion 6 paraphrased (not elated at another's excellence; the horse saying 'I am beautiful'; the use of appearances in accord with nature). Confirm.
Greek χρῆσις φαντασιῶν, 'use of impressions': confirm transliteration and that it appears in Enchiridion 6.
The car, college and team examples are modern illustrations.
